## 1 · Right-angle conditions

*Seeds: 2022 P2 Q11, plus a real cross-exam problem (MAT 2019 Q1H).*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — "when is this angle $90^\circ$?"

A right angle is never really a geometry fact to *see*; it is an **equation to write**. Same three moves every
time:

1. **Name the triangle at that vertex.** Call the two sides leaving the vertex the **legs**, and the side
   opposite the **hypotenuse**.
2. **Right angle $\Leftrightarrow$ Pythagoras:** $\ \text{leg}_1^{2}+\text{leg}_2^{2}=\text{hypotenuse}^{2}$.
   Write it and simplify — the equation you get **is** the necessary-and-sufficient condition.
3. **If a perpendicular drops from the right angle onto the hypotenuse, use the geometric mean.** With the
   foot splitting the hypotenuse into $p$ and $q$ and altitude $h$:
   $$h^{2}=pq,\qquad \text{leg}^{2}=(\text{adjacent segment})\times(\text{hypotenuse}).$$

**Two shortcuts.** In coordinates, perpendicular $\Leftrightarrow$ **dot product $=0$** $\Leftrightarrow$
**product of gradients $=-1$**. And the locus of all $P$ with $\angle APB=90^\circ$ is the **circle on $AB$ as
diameter** (angle in a semicircle — Thales).

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
A=np.array([0,0]); B=np.array([13,0]); D=np.array([4,0]); C=np.array([4,6])
plt.figure(figsize=(5.4,3.1))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([C[0],D[0]],[C[1],D[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.5)
u=(A-C)/np.hypot(*(A-C)); v=(B-C)/np.hypot(*(B-C)); srt=0.8
cor=np.array([C+srt*u, C+srt*u+srt*v, C+srt*v]); plt.plot(cor[:,0],cor[:,1],color='0.4',lw=1)
plt.plot([D[0],D[0]+0.5,D[0]+0.5],[0.5,0.5,0],color='0.4',lw=1)
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-12,-3)),(B,'B',(6,-3)),(C,'C',(-4,8)),(D,'D',(-4,-16))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('p',(2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-15),fontsize=10,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('q',(8.5,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-15),fontsize=10,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('h',(4,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,0),fontsize=10,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('leg',(2,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-26,0),fontsize=9,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.annotate('leg',(8.5,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,4),fontsize=9,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('h² = p·q   and   leg² = (adjacent segment) × hypotenuse',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- Right angle test: use **Pythagoras**, **dot product $=0$**, or **gradient product $=-1$**.
- If an altitude from the right angle hits the hypotenuse, memorise
  $$h^{2}=pq,\qquad \text{leg}^{2}=(\text{adjacent hypotenuse segment})(\text{whole hypotenuse}).$$
- Locus fact: $\angle APB=90^\circ$ means $P$ lies on the **circle with $AB$ as diameter**.
- "Necessary and sufficient" means your final condition must work in **both** directions.
- **Extra practice:** PAT Maths and MAT Section A for circle/coordinate-geometry versions; ECAA Advanced Maths
  for speed drills.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter. Locus → an equation. Length → exact surd. "Is it a right angle?" → yes/no
with the check.
:::

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q11 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
Kite $PQRS$ has perpendicular diagonals meeting at $O$, with $OP=OR=x$, $OQ=y$, $OS=z$. What is the
**necessary and sufficient** condition for $\angle SPQ$ to be a right angle?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $x=y=z$ &nbsp; **B** $2x=y+z$ &nbsp; **C** $x^{2}=yz$ &nbsp; **D** $y=z$ &nbsp;
**E** $y^{2}=x^{2}+z^{2}$
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x,y,z=2.0,1.0,4.0
P,Q,R,S=np.array([-x,0]),np.array([0,-y]),np.array([x,0]),np.array([0,z])
plt.figure(figsize=(3.2,3.9))
poly=np.array([P,S,R,Q,P]); plt.plot(poly[:,0],poly[:,1],'-o',color='#2b6cb0')
plt.plot([P[0],R[0]],[0,0],':',color='0.6'); plt.plot([0,0],[Q[1],S[1]],':',color='0.6')
plt.plot([-0.35,-0.35,0],[0,0.35,0.35],color='0.4',lw=1)
for pt,nm,off in [(P,'P',(-14,2)),(Q,'Q',(4,-12)),(R,'R',(6,2)),(S,'S',(4,6)),(np.zeros(2),'O',(6,-13))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('x',(-x/2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(0,4),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('x',(x/2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(0,4),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('y',(0,-y/2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,0),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('z',(0,z/2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,0),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('kite PQRS, diagonals ⊥ at O;  ∠SPQ = ?',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Move 1–2 (Pythagoras).** The sides at $P$ are $SP=\sqrt{x^{2}+z^{2}}$ and $PQ=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$; the
opposite side is $SQ=y+z$. If the angle at $P$ is the right angle, then $SQ$ is the hypotenuse, so Pythagoras
is exactly the test we need:
$$\angle SPQ=90^\circ\iff SP^{2}+PQ^{2}=SQ^{2}\iff (x^{2}+z^{2})+(x^{2}+y^{2})=(y+z)^{2}\iff x^{2}=yz.$$
The word **necessary and sufficient** is important: the algebra above is an "if and only if", so $x^{2}=yz$
is not merely a consequence of the right angle; it is exactly the condition for the right angle.

**Move 3 (geometric mean).** There is also a very quick right-triangle fact here. $PO=x$ is the altitude from
the right angle $P$ to the hypotenuse $SQ$, split into $OS=z$ and $OQ=y$, so the altitude rule gives
$x^{2}=zy$ directly. Answer **C**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x,y,z=2.0,1.0,4.0
P,Q,R,S=np.array([-x,0]),np.array([0,-y]),np.array([x,0]),np.array([0,z])
plt.figure(figsize=(3.4,4.0))
poly=np.array([P,S,R,Q,P]); plt.plot(poly[:,0],poly[:,1],'-o',color='#2b6cb0')
plt.plot([P[0],R[0]],[0,0],':',color='0.6'); plt.plot([0,0],[Q[1],S[1]],':',color='0.6')
for pt,nm in [(P,'P'),(Q,'Q'),(R,'R'),(S,'S'),(np.zeros(2),'O')]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,4))
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.title('x²=yz ⟺ ∠SPQ = 90°',fontsize=9); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(compute the geometric mean)*

::: {.question}
In a right-angled triangle the altitude from the right angle meets the hypotenuse and splits it into segments
of length $4$ and $9$. Find the altitude $h$, and the two legs.

*Answer form: exact surds.*
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
A=np.array([0,0]); B=np.array([13,0]); D=np.array([4,0]); C=np.array([4,6])
plt.figure(figsize=(5.0,2.9))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([C[0],D[0]],[C[1],D[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.4)
u=(A-C)/np.hypot(*(A-C)); v=(B-C)/np.hypot(*(B-C)); srt=0.8
cor=np.array([C+srt*u, C+srt*u+srt*v, C+srt*v]); plt.plot(cor[:,0],cor[:,1],color='0.4',lw=1)
plt.plot([D[0],D[0]+0.5,D[0]+0.5],[0.5,0.5,0],color='0.4',lw=1)
plt.annotate('4',(2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-15),fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('9',(8.5,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-15),fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('h = ?',(4,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,0),fontsize=10,color='crimson')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('altitude to the hypotenuse splits it into 4 and 9 — find h and the two legs',fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
The key picture is a right triangle with an altitude dropped to the hypotenuse. In that picture, the altitude
is the geometric mean of the two pieces of the hypotenuse:
$$h^{2}=pq=4\times9=36\Rightarrow h=6.$$
The whole hypotenuse is $c=4+9=13$. Each leg is also a geometric mean: take the segment of the hypotenuse next
to that leg, multiply by the whole hypotenuse, then square-root:
$$\text{leg}_1=\sqrt{4\times13}=2\sqrt{13},\qquad \text{leg}_2=\sqrt{9\times13}=3\sqrt{13}.$$
The final answer is therefore
$$\boxed{h=6,\quad \text{legs }2\sqrt{13}\text{ and }3\sqrt{13}}.$$
Quick check: $(2\sqrt{13})^2+(3\sqrt{13})^2=52+117=169=13^2$, so the lengths are consistent.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
A=np.array([0,0]); B=np.array([13,0]); D=np.array([4,0]); C=np.array([4,6])
plt.figure(figsize=(5.2,3.0))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([C[0],D[0]],[C[1],D[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.5)
plt.plot([D[0],D[0]+0.5,D[0]+0.5],[0.5,0.5,0],color='0.4',lw=1)
plt.annotate('4',(2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-15),fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('9',(8.5,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-15),fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('h=6',(4,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,0),fontsize=10,color='crimson')
plt.annotate('2√13',(1.6,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-34,0),fontsize=9,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.annotate('3√13',(8.5,3),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,4),fontsize=9,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('segments 4 and 9  →  h=√(4·9)=6,  legs 2√13 and 3√13',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(the semicircle / Thales locus)*

::: {.question}
$A$ and $B$ are fixed points. Describe the set of all points $P$ for which $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ &nbsp; **B** the circle with $AB$ as diameter &nbsp;
**C** the circle centred at $A$ through $B$ &nbsp; **D** a single point &nbsp; **E** the line through $A$ and $B$
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
A=np.array([-2,0]); B=np.array([2,0]); P=np.array([-0.9,np.sqrt(4-0.9**2)])
plt.figure(figsize=(4.0,2.9))
plt.plot(*A,'ks'); plt.plot(*B,'ks'); plt.plot(*P,'o',color='crimson')
plt.plot([P[0],A[0]],[P[1],A[1]],color='crimson',lw=1)
plt.plot([P[0],B[0]],[P[1],B[1]],color='crimson',lw=1)
u=(A-P)/np.hypot(*(A-P)); v=(B-P)/np.hypot(*(B-P)); srt=0.30
cor=np.array([P+srt*u, P+srt*u+srt*v, P+srt*v]); plt.plot(cor[:,0],cor[:,1],color='0.4',lw=1)
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-12,-4)),(B,'B',(6,-4)),(P,'P',(-4,8))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('∠APB = 90°',P,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(12,-12),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('A, B fixed;  P moves keeping ∠APB = 90°.  What path does P trace?',fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: B.** Keep $A$ and $B$ fixed, and imagine moving $P$ around. The segment $AB$ is being viewed from
$P$, so $\angle APB$ is the angle *subtended by $AB$* at $P$.

Thales' theorem says that every point on the circle with $AB$ as diameter sees $AB$ under a right angle. The
converse is just as useful here: if $\angle APB=90^\circ$, then $P$ must lie on that same circle. So the locus
is **the circle with $AB$ as diameter** — centre the midpoint of $AB$, radius $\tfrac12 AB$.

This is the geometric-mean condition in disguise: dropping the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$ gives
$h^{2}=(\text{foot to }A)(\text{foot to }B)$, exactly the circle equation.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
th=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,300)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.4,3.4))
plt.plot(np.cos(th),np.sin(th),color='#2b6cb0')
A=np.array([-1,0]); B=np.array([1,0])
plt.plot(*A,'ks'); plt.plot(*B,'ks')
plt.annotate('A',A,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-12,-4))
plt.annotate('B',B,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,-4))
for ang,col in [(55,'crimson'),(100,'#dd6b20'),(140,'#2ca02c')]:
    P=np.array([np.cos(np.radians(ang)),np.sin(np.radians(ang))])
    plt.plot([P[0],A[0]],[P[1],A[1]],color=col,lw=1)
    plt.plot([P[0],B[0]],[P[1],B[1]],color=col,lw=1)
    plt.plot(*P,'o',color=col,ms=4)
plt.plot([-1,1],[0,0],color='0.6',lw=0.8); plt.plot(0,0,'k+')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('every P on the circle sees AB at 90°  (AB = diameter)',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(coordinate version — write the locus)*

::: {.question}
$A=(0,0)$ and $B=(8,0)$. Find the equation of the locus of points $P=(x,y)$ with $\angle APB=90^\circ$.

*Answer form: an equation of a circle.*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Dot-product route.** A right angle is a perpendicularity test, and in coordinates that means "dot product
zero". From $P=(x,y)$,
$$\vec{PA}=(-x,-y),\qquad \vec{PB}=(8-x,-y).$$
So
$$(-x)(8-x)+(-y)(-y)=0\Rightarrow x^{2}-8x+y^{2}=0\Rightarrow (x-4)^{2}+y^{2}=16.$$
This is the circle on $AB$ as diameter (centre $(4,0)$, radius $4$) — matching Problem 3.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
th=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,300)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,3.0))
plt.plot(4+4*np.cos(th),4*np.sin(th),color='#2b6cb0')
A,B=np.array([0,0]),np.array([8,0]); plt.plot(*A,'ks'); plt.plot(*B,'ks')
plt.annotate('A',A,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-12,-2)); plt.annotate('B',B,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,-2))
P=np.array([4,4]); plt.plot(*P,'o',color='crimson'); plt.annotate('P',P,textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,4),color='crimson')
plt.plot([P[0],A[0]],[P[1],A[1]],color='crimson',lw=1); plt.plot([P[0],B[0]],[P[1],B[1]],color='crimson',lw=1)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.title('∠APB=90° ⟺ P on (x−4)²+y²=16',fontsize=9); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(read a leg off the segments)*

::: {.question}
A right-angled triangle has legs $5$ and $12$. The altitude from the right angle meets the hypotenuse at $D$.
Find the two segments the foot $D$ makes on the hypotenuse, and the altitude.

*Answer form: three exact fractions.*
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C=np.array([0,0]); A=np.array([0,5]); B=np.array([12,0])
AB=B-A; t=np.dot(C-A,AB)/np.dot(AB,AB); Dp=A+t*AB
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,3.2))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([C[0],Dp[0]],[C[1],Dp[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.4)
plt.plot([0.7,0.7,0],[0,0.7,0.7],color='0.4',lw=1)
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-12,2)),(B,'B',(6,-2)),(C,'C',(-13,-10)),(Dp,'D',(4,8))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('5',(0,2.5),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-12,0),fontsize=10,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.annotate('12',(6,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-4,-15),fontsize=10,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('legs 5 and 12; altitude foot D on the hypotenuse — find the segments and the altitude',fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Hypotenuse $c=\sqrt{5^{2}+12^{2}}=13$. Each leg is the geometric mean of its adjacent segment and $c$, so the
segment adjacent to a leg is $\dfrac{\text{leg}^{2}}{c}$:
$$p=\frac{5^{2}}{13}=\frac{25}{13},\qquad q=\frac{12^{2}}{13}=\frac{144}{13}\quad\Big(p+q=\tfrac{169}{13}=13\ \checkmark\Big).$$
Altitude $h=\sqrt{pq}=\dfrac{5\times12}{13}=\dfrac{60}{13}$ (or "area twice over": $\tfrac12\cdot5\cdot12=\tfrac12\cdot13\cdot h$).
:::

### Problem 6 &nbsp; *(test for a right angle — the converse)*

::: {.question}
In triangle $ABC$, the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $BD=2$, $DC=8$ and $AD=4$.
Is angle $BAC$ a right angle? Justify with a single equation.
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
B=np.array([0,0]); C=np.array([10,0]); D=np.array([2,0]); A=np.array([2,4])
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,2.9))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([A[0],D[0]],[A[1],D[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.4)
plt.plot([D[0],D[0]+0.5,D[0]+0.5],[0.5,0.5,0],color='0.4',lw=1)
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-2,8)),(B,'B',(-12,-4)),(C,'C',(6,-4)),(D,'D',(-2,-15))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('2',(1,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-14),fontsize=9)
plt.annotate('8',(6,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-2,-14),fontsize=9)
plt.annotate('4',(2,2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,0),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('AD ⊥ BC with BD=2, DC=8, AD=4.  Is ∠BAC = 90°?',fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Use the **converse** of the geometric-mean rule: $\angle BAC=90^\circ$ **iff** the altitude to $BC$ satisfies
$AD^{2}=BD\cdot DC$. Here
$$AD^{2}=4^{2}=16,\qquad BD\cdot DC=2\times8=16,$$
so $AD^{2}=BD\cdot DC$ and angle $BAC$ **is** a right angle. (If instead $AD^{2}<BD\cdot DC$ the angle would be
obtuse; if $>$, acute — the same equation grades the angle.)

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
B=np.array([0,0]); C=np.array([10,0]); D=np.array([2,0]); A=np.array([2,4])
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,2.8))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([A[0],D[0]],[A[1],D[1]],'--',color='crimson')
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(0,6)),(B,'B',(-12,-4)),(C,'C',(6,-4)),(D,'D',(-2,-14))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off)
plt.annotate('BD=2',(1,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-6,4),fontsize=8)
plt.annotate('DC=8',(6,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-6,4),fontsize=8)
plt.annotate('AD=4',(2,2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,0),fontsize=8,color='crimson')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off'); plt.title('AD²=BD·DC ⟹ ∠BAC = 90°',fontsize=9); plt.show()
```

### Problem 7 &nbsp; *(MAT 2019 Q1H — real past paper)*

::: {.question}
The triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and the side lengths are positive numbers in **geometric
progression**. It follows that $\tan\angle BAC$ is either

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** $\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}}$ or $\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(b)** $\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\sqrt3}{2}}$ or $\sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{2}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(c)** $\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}}$ or $\sqrt{\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(d)** $-\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}}$ or $\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}}$ &nbsp;&nbsp;
**(e)** $\sqrt{\dfrac{1+\sqrt3}{2}}$ or $\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\sqrt3}{2}}$
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
phi=(1+5**0.5)/2; r=phi**0.5
B=np.array([0,0]); A=np.array([0,1]); C=np.array([r,0])
plt.figure(figsize=(3.8,3.0))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([0,0.12,0.12],[0.12,0.12,0],color='0.4',lw=1)
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-14,0)),(B,'B',(-14,-10)),(C,'C',(6,-4))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.annotate('a',(0,0.5),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-10,0),fontsize=10,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.annotate('ar',(r/2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-4,-14),fontsize=10,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.annotate('ar²',(r/2,0.5),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,4),fontsize=10,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('right angle at B; sides a, ar, ar² in geometric progression.  tan∠BAC = ?',fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Same move: right angle $\to$ Pythagoras.** Write the sides as $a,\,ar,\,ar^{2}$ (a geometric progression).
The right angle is at $B$, so the **hypotenuse** $AC$ is the longest side $ar^{2}$, and the legs are $a$ and
$ar$. Pythagoras:
$$(ar^{2})^{2}=a^{2}+(ar)^{2}\;\Rightarrow\;r^{4}=1+r^{2}\;\Rightarrow\;r^{4}-r^{2}-1=0\;\Rightarrow\;r^{2}=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}=\varphi\ \text{(the golden ratio)}.$$
$\tan\angle BAC=\dfrac{\text{opposite leg}}{\text{adjacent leg}}$ is the ratio of the two legs — either $r$ or
$\tfrac1r$, depending on which leg is opposite $A$:
$$r=\sqrt{\varphi}=\sqrt{\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad \frac1r=\sqrt{\tfrac1\varphi}=\sqrt{\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2}}\quad\Big(\tfrac1\varphi=\varphi-1=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{2}\Big).$$
Both are positive, so the answer is **(c)**. *(Fast elimination: a tangent of an acute angle is positive and
real, which instantly kills (a), (d), (e); and the golden-ratio equation rules out the $\sqrt3$ option (b).)*

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
phi=(1+5**0.5)/2; r=phi**0.5
B=np.array([0,0]); A=np.array([0,1]); C=np.array([r,0])   # legs AB=1, BC=√φ, hyp AC=φ
plt.figure(figsize=(3.8,3.0))
tri=np.array([A,B,C,A]); plt.plot(tri[:,0],tri[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([0,0.12,0.12],[0.12,0.12,0],color='0.4',lw=1)   # right-angle mark at B
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-14,0)),(B,'B',(-14,-10)),(C,'C',(6,-4))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off)
plt.annotate('1',(0,0.5),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-10,0),fontsize=9)
plt.annotate('√φ',(r/2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-4,-14),fontsize=9)
plt.annotate('φ (hyp)',(r/2,0.5),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,4),fontsize=9,color='#2b6cb0')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('sides 1, √φ, φ  (r²=φ);  tan∠BAC = √φ or 1/√φ',fontsize=8.5); plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Memorise — right-angle conditions

| Fact | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Pythagoras (both ways)** | $\angle$ at a vertex is $90^\circ\iff\text{leg}^2+\text{leg}^2=\text{hyp}^2$ |
| **Altitude = geometric mean** | altitude to hypotenuse: $h^{2}=pq$ (segments $p,q$) |
| **Leg = geometric mean** | $\text{leg}^{2}=(\text{adjacent segment})\times(\text{hypotenuse})$ |
| **Angle grader** | $AD^{2}=BD\cdot DC\Rightarrow 90^\circ$; $\;<\Rightarrow$ obtuse; $\;>\Rightarrow$ acute |
| **Thales locus** | $\{P:\angle APB=90^\circ\}$ = circle on $AB$ as diameter |
| **Coordinates** | perpendicular $\iff$ dot product $=0\iff$ gradients multiply to $-1$ |

**One line to carry:** a right angle is an **equation** — Pythagoras, or the geometric mean $h^{2}=pq$.
:::

### Problem 8 &nbsp; *(ECAA Specimen — altitude to the hypotenuse)*

::: {.question}
*Adapted from ECAA Specimen, Section 1 Part A, Question 2.*

In a right-angled triangle $PQR$, the hypotenuse is $PR$. The side $PQ$ has length $20$, and
$RQ:PQ=1:2$. Find the length of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the hypotenuse $PR$.

*Answer form: exact surd.*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: $4\sqrt5$.**

**Step 1 — get the three sides.** Since $RQ:PQ=1:2$ and $PQ=20$, we have $RQ=10$. The hypotenuse is
$$PR=\sqrt{20^2+10^2}=\sqrt{500}=10\sqrt5.$$

**Step 2 — use area two ways.** If the perpendicular from $Q$ to $PR$ is $h$, then
$$\frac12(20)(10)=\frac12(10\sqrt5)h.$$
So
$$100=5\sqrt5\,h\Rightarrow h=\frac{20}{\sqrt5}=4\sqrt5.$$

This is the same altitude-to-hypotenuse idea as the TMUA kite question, just with ordinary side lengths.
:::

:::

## 2 · Necessary, sufficient & "must it be true?"

*Seeds: 2022 P2 Q4, Q6, Q19.*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — necessary, sufficient, and "must it be true?"

Every one of these questions is secretly the same question: **does the arrow $P\Rightarrow Q$ hold?** Five
steps:

1. **Turn the words into an arrow.**
   - "$P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$" means $P\Rightarrow Q$ (P is *enough*).
   - "$P$ is **necessary** for $Q$" means $Q\Rightarrow P$ (Q can't happen without P).
   - "**Must** $Q$ be true, given $P$?" is just "is $P\Rightarrow Q$ true?"
   - "**Necessary and sufficient**" means $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ — *both* arrows.
2. **To break an arrow, hunt one counterexample.** Find a single object with the hypothesis **true** and the
   conclusion **false**. That one example settles it — no proof needed.
3. **Reach for the most flexible / degenerate shape first.** A **rectangle** (not a square), an **isosceles**
   case, $n=4$, $x=0$, a boundary value. These are where "equal $\Rightarrow$ regular / special" usually
   breaks.
4. **To confirm an arrow, prove it in general** — represent the objects generally and show it always holds.
5. **For "necessary *and* sufficient", test the two directions separately.** One can hold while the other
   fails.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Worked idea.** *"$n$ triangles of equal area from the centre $\Rightarrow$ the polygon is regular?"* Don't
prove — **test $n=4$ first**: a non-square **rectangle** is cyclic, its four centre-triangles have equal area
(opposite ones are congruent, and $\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$ makes the adjacent pair equal too), yet
it is not regular. Counterexample found — so it is **not** sufficient for $n=4$.
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
th=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,200)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.8,3.2))
ax[0].plot(2*np.cos(th),1.6*np.sin(th),color='#2b6cb0')
ax[0].plot(0.9*np.cos(th)-0.4,0.7*np.sin(th),color='#dd6b20')
ax[0].text(-0.4,0,'P',ha='center',va='center',color='#dd6b20',fontsize=12)
ax[0].text(1.25,1.05,'Q',ha='center',va='center',color='#2b6cb0',fontsize=12)
ax[0].set_title('P sufficient for Q:  P ⇒ Q\n(being in P is enough to be in Q)',fontsize=9)
ax[1].plot(2*np.cos(th),1.6*np.sin(th),color='#dd6b20')
ax[1].plot(0.9*np.cos(th)-0.4,0.7*np.sin(th),color='#2b6cb0')
ax[1].text(-0.4,0,'Q',ha='center',va='center',color='#2b6cb0',fontsize=12)
ax[1].text(1.25,1.05,'P',ha='center',va='center',color='#dd6b20',fontsize=12)
ax[1].set_title('P necessary for Q:  Q ⇒ P\n(no Q without P)',fontsize=9)
for a in ax: a.set_aspect('equal'); a.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- $P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$ means $P\Rightarrow Q$: having $P$ is enough.
- $P$ is **necessary** for $Q$ means $Q\Rightarrow P$: no $Q$ without $P$.
- To disprove sufficiency, find $P$ true and $Q$ false.
- To disprove necessity, find $Q$ true and $P$ false.
- For "must be true" questions, one counterexample destroys a proposed must-hold statement.
- **Extra practice:** TMUA Logic and Proof notes first; then FP1/FP2 proof sections and STEP Foundation for
  more iff/counterexample practice.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter, or "necessary / sufficient / both / neither", with the counterexample or
the proof.
:::

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q19 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
A polygon ($n\ge3$) has all vertices on a circle with the centre inside, and the radii cut it into $n$
triangles of **equal area**. For which $n$ are these properties **sufficient** to force the polygon to be
regular?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** no $n$ &nbsp; **B** $n=3$ only &nbsp; **C** $n=3,4$ only &nbsp; **D** $n=3$ and $n\ge5$ only
&nbsp; **E** all $n$
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
th=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,300)
plt.figure(figsize=(3.6,3.6))
plt.plot(np.cos(th),np.sin(th),color='0.7')
angs=[90,160,215,300,20]
pts=np.array([[np.cos(np.radians(a)),np.sin(np.radians(a))] for a in angs])
poly=np.vstack([pts,pts[0]]); plt.plot(poly[:,0],poly[:,1],'-o',color='#2b6cb0')
for pt in pts: plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],':',color='crimson')
plt.plot(0,0,'ks')
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('vertices on a circle; radii cut it into n triangles (here n=5).\nWhen do equal areas force the polygon to be regular?',fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: B ($n=3$ only).**

**Step 1 — set up the central angles.** Let $O$ be the centre and $A_1,\dots,A_n$ the consecutive vertices,
and write $\theta_i=\angle A_iOA_{i+1}$ for the central angle of the $i$-th triangle. Since $O$ is inside,
$0<\theta_i<180^\circ$, and one full turn gives $\theta_1+\dots+\theta_n=360^\circ$.

**Step 2 — area of each slice.** Every triangle has two sides equal to the radius $R$, so
$$\text{Area}_i=\tfrac12 R^{2}\sin\theta_i.$$

**Step 3 — equal areas $\iff$ equal sines.** Equal areas mean $\sin\theta_1=\sin\theta_2=\dots=\sin\theta_n$.
But on $0<\theta<180^\circ$, $\ \sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$, so each $\theta_i$ is $x$ **or**
$180^\circ-x$ for a single value $x$. *(This ambiguity is the whole crack.)*

**Step 4 — $n=3$ is forced regular.** Three angles, each $x$ or $180^\circ-x$, summing to $360^\circ$:

- all three $x$: $\ 3x=360^\circ\Rightarrow x=120^\circ$ — an equilateral (regular) triangle. ✔
- $x,x,180^\circ-x$: $\ 2x+(180^\circ-x)=360^\circ\Rightarrow x=180^\circ$ — impossible.
- $x,180^\circ-x,180^\circ-x$: $\ x+2(180^\circ-x)=360^\circ\Rightarrow x=0^\circ$ — impossible.

So the only possibility is $\theta_1=\theta_2=\theta_3=120^\circ$, hence **$n=3\Rightarrow$ necessarily regular.**

**Step 5 — $n=4$ counterexample.** Take central angles $60^\circ,120^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ$ (sum
$360^\circ$). Since $\sin60^\circ=\sin120^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, all four triangles have the **same** area
$\tfrac12 R^{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$; but $60^\circ\ne120^\circ$, so the sides alternate and the polygon is
**not** regular — it is a rectangle that is not a square.

**Step 6 — $n=5$ counterexample.** Take $60^\circ,60^\circ,60^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ$ (sum $360^\circ$).
Again $\sin60^\circ=\sin120^\circ$, so all areas are equal, yet $60^\circ\ne120^\circ$ means the sides are not
all equal — not a regular pentagon.

**Conclusion.** Only $n=3$ forces the polygon to be regular, so the answer is **B**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
th=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,300)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.8,3.6))
def draw(a,angs,title):
    a.plot(np.cos(th),np.sin(th),color='0.7')
    cum=np.cumsum([0]+angs[:-1])
    V=np.array([[np.cos(np.radians(c)),np.sin(np.radians(c))] for c in cum])
    poly=np.vstack([V,V[0]]); a.plot(poly[:,0],poly[:,1],'-o',color='#2b6cb0')
    for p in V: a.plot([0,p[0]],[0,p[1]],':',color='crimson')
    a.plot(0,0,'ks'); a.set_aspect('equal'); a.axis('off'); a.set_title(title,fontsize=8)
draw(ax[0],[60,120,60,120],'n=4:  60°,120°,60°,120°\nsin60°=sin120° ⟹ equal areas,\nbut 60°≠120° ⟹ NOT regular\n(rectangle, not square)')
draw(ax[1],[60,60,60,60,120],'n=5:  60°,60°,60°,60°,120°\nequal areas, yet 60°≠120°\n⟹ NOT a regular pentagon')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q6 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
A list of $n$ integers. Let $P$ be "$n$ is odd" and $Q$ be "the median of the list is one of the numbers in
the list". Which is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $P$ is necessary and sufficient for $Q$ &nbsp; **B** necessary, not sufficient &nbsp;
**C** sufficient, not necessary &nbsp; **D** neither
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: C (sufficient, not necessary).**

**Step 1 — the two arrows to test.** Sufficient asks $P\Rightarrow Q$; necessary asks $Q\Rightarrow P$.

**Step 2 — is $P\Rightarrow Q$? (sufficient).** If $n$ is odd, the median is the single **middle** entry of
the sorted list, which *is* one of the numbers. So $P\Rightarrow Q$ — **sufficient**. ✔

**Step 3 — is $Q\Rightarrow P$? (necessary).** Find a counterexample: an even-length list whose median is
still in the list. Take $1,2,2,3$ ($n=4$, even): median $=\tfrac{2+2}{2}=2$, which **is** in the list. So $Q$
holds with $P$ false — **not necessary**. ✘

So $P$ is sufficient but not necessary.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q4 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
A circle has equation $x^{2}+2fx+y^{2}+2gy+h=0$, and $P=(p,q)$ is a point. Let $L$ be the distance from the
**centre** of the circle to $P$. Which one set of data is, on its own, **sufficient** to find $L$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f,g,h$ &nbsp; **B** $f,g,p,q$ &nbsp; **C** $f,h,p,q$ &nbsp; **D** $g,h,p,q$ &nbsp;
**E** none of A–D
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: B ($f,g,p,q$).**

**Step 1 — what does $L$ actually depend on?** $L$ is the distance from the **centre** to $P$ — so you need
the centre and $P$, nothing else.

**Step 2 — find the centre.** Completing the square, $x^{2}+2fx+y^{2}+2gy+h=0$ has centre $(-f,-g)$. So the
centre needs only $f$ and $g$; the constant $h$ sets the **radius**, which is irrelevant to $L$.

**Step 3 — assemble.** $L=\sqrt{(p+f)^{2}+(q+g)^{2}}$ needs exactly $f,g$ (centre) and $p,q$ (the point). That
is set **B**. (Any set missing $f$ or $g$ can't locate the centre; any set carrying $h$ carries a red herring.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}

:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(is the condition sufficient? — a shape counterexample)*

::: {.question}
Is "a quadrilateral has **equal diagonals**" **sufficient** for it to be a **rectangle**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: No — not sufficient.**

**Step 1 — the arrow.** Sufficient would mean: equal diagonals $\Rightarrow$ rectangle.

**Step 2 — hunt the flexible counterexample.** An **isosceles trapezium** (non-rectangular) has equal
diagonals, yet it is not a rectangle. One counterexample kills sufficiency. (A rectangle *does* have equal
diagonals, so "equal diagonals" is **necessary** — but not sufficient.)

**Step 3 — what would be sufficient?** "Equal diagonals **that bisect each other**" forces a rectangle. The
extra clause is exactly what the trapezium lacks.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
A=np.array([-2,0]); B=np.array([2,0]); C=np.array([1,2]); D=np.array([-1,2])
plt.figure(figsize=(4.4,3.0))
quad=np.array([A,B,C,D,A]); plt.plot(quad[:,0],quad[:,1],color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot([A[0],C[0]],[A[1],C[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.5)
plt.plot([B[0],D[0]],[B[1],D[1]],'--',color='crimson',lw=1.5)
for pt,nm,off in [(A,'A',(-12,-4)),(B,'B',(6,-4)),(C,'C',(6,2)),(D,'D',(-12,2))]:
    plt.annotate(nm,pt,textcoords='offset points',xytext=off,fontsize=10)
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal'); plt.axis('off')
plt.title('isosceles trapezium: diagonals equal (√13 = √13)\nyet it is NOT a rectangle',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(a "one condition isn't enough" trap)*

::: {.question}
Is "$b^{2}-4ac<0$" **sufficient**, on its own, for "$ax^{2}+bx+c>0$ for all real $x$"?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: No — you also need $a>0$.**

**Step 1 — what does $b^{2}-4ac<0$ give?** It says the quadratic has **no real roots**, so it never touches
the $x$-axis — it stays entirely **above** or entirely **below** it.

**Step 2 — which side? That's the sign of $a$.** With $a>0$ the parabola opens up (stays above); with $a<0$ it
opens down (stays below).

**Step 3 — counterexample.** $-x^{2}-1$: here $a=-1,b=0,c=-1$, so $b^{2}-4ac=-4<0$, yet $-x^{2}-1<0$ for all
$x$. So $b^{2}-4ac<0$ alone is **not** sufficient — the necessary-and-sufficient condition is
$$a>0\ \textbf{and}\ b^{2}-4ac<0.$$

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-3,3,300)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0,2.8))
ax.plot(x,x**2+1,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='a=+1: x²+1 > 0 ✓')
ax.plot(x,-x**2-1,color='#dd6b20',lw=2,label='a=−1: −x²−1 < 0 ✗')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8); ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
ax.set_title('both have b²−4ac<0; the sign of a decides',fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 6 &nbsp; *(necessary vs sufficient — tell them apart)*

::: {.question}
For the statement "$x^{2}>4$", classify the condition "$x>2$": is it **necessary**, **sufficient**, **both**,
or **neither**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: sufficient, not necessary.**

**Step 1 — sufficient? ($x>2\Rightarrow x^{2}>4$).** If $x>2$ then $x^{2}>4$ — true. So $x>2$ is
**sufficient**. ✔

**Step 2 — necessary? ($x^{2}>4\Rightarrow x>2$).** Counterexample $x=-3$: $x^{2}=9>4$ but $x>2$ is false. So
$x>2$ is **not necessary**. ✘

**Step 3 — the full picture.** $x^{2}>4\iff x>2$ **or** $x<-2$. So "$x>2$" is only *one branch* — enough to
force $x^{2}>4$, but not required. (The necessary-and-sufficient condition is "$x>2$ or $x<-2$", i.e.
$\lvert x\rvert>2$.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Memorise — necessary / sufficient / must it be true?

| Words | Arrow |
|---|---|
| $P$ **sufficient** for $Q$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ (P is enough) |
| $P$ **necessary** for $Q$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ (Q needs P) |
| "**Must** $Q$ hold, given $P$?" | is $P\Rightarrow Q$ true? |
| **Necessary and sufficient** | $P\Leftrightarrow Q$ (both arrows) |

- **To break an arrow:** one counterexample (hypothesis true, conclusion false) is enough — reach for the
  **rectangle / isosceles / $n=4$ / $x=0$ / boundary** first.
- **Equal areas or equal sines** hide the trap $\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$ — the angles can differ.
- **"Positive for all $x$"** needs *both* $a>0$ **and** $b^{2}-4ac<0$ — one alone is never enough.
- A condition can be **necessary but not sufficient** (equal diagonals for a rectangle) or **sufficient but
  not necessary** ($x>2$ for $x^{2}>4$). Always test **both** directions.
:::

## 3 · Graph-matching & nested functions

*Seeds: 2022 P2 Q18, Q20, plus a real cross-exam problem (MAT 2019 Q1C).*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — pin a curve by its ends and its turning point

Don't differentiate all the options. Fix each curve with two quick reads:

1. **Endpoints** — the value or limit at each end of the domain ($x\to0$, $x\to\tfrac\pi2$, $x\to\pm\infty$).
2. **The turning point** — roughly *where* the max/min sits. For any $t^{t}$ (or $f^{f}$) the minimum is at
   $t=\dfrac1e\approx0.37$, value $\left(\tfrac1e\right)^{1/e}\approx0.69$; on $[0,1]$ it starts and ends at
   $1$ (a shallow U).

And if the expression is **nested or disguised, rewrite it first**: a geometric series
$\sin^{2}x+\sin^{4}x+\dots=\dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{1-\sin^{2}x}=\tan^{2}x$; a chain of $\cos/\sin$ — track the
**range** through each layer.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t=np.linspace(1e-4,1,400); y=t**t
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,3.0)); plt.plot(t,y,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
tm=1/np.e; plt.plot(tm,tm**tm,'o',color='crimson')
plt.annotate('min ≈ 0.69\nat t = 1/e ≈ 0.37',(tm,tm**tm),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(14,-6),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.plot(0,1,'ks',ms=4); plt.plot(1,1,'ks',ms=4)
plt.annotate('→ 1',(0,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,-1),fontsize=9)
plt.annotate('1',(1,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(4,-2),fontsize=9)
plt.ylim(0.6,1.05); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.xlabel('t'); plt.ylabel('t^t')
plt.title('The t^t template: shallow U, both ends → 1',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- The template $t^t$ on $0<t\le1$ starts near $1$, ends at $1$, and has its minimum at
  $$t=\frac1e,\qquad t^t=\left(\frac1e\right)^{1/e}\approx0.69.$$
- To differentiate $t^t$, do **log differentiation**: write $t^t=e^{t\ln t}$, so
  $$(t^t)'=t^t(\ln t+1).$$
- For nested trig maxima, track the **range after each layer**. $\cos u$ reaches $1$ only if $u=0$; $\sin u$
  is increasing on $[-1,1]$.
- For graph matching, endpoints and special values usually beat full algebra.
- **Extra practice:** MAT Section A for graph matching; PAT/ENGAA Maths for functions, transformations, and
  solution-counting.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter. "How many solutions" → a whole number.
:::

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q18 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
$P,Q,R,S$ (below) are the graphs of
$$y=(\cos x)^{\cos x},\quad y=(\sin x)^{\sin x},\quad y=(\cos x)^{\sin x},\quad y=(\sin x)^{\cos x}$$
on $0<x<\tfrac\pi2$, **in some order**. Which row of the table correctly identifies the graphs?
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0.001,np.pi/2-0.001,400)
sk=[('P',np.cos(x)**np.sin(x)),('Q',np.sin(x)**np.cos(x)),
    ('R',np.cos(x)**np.cos(x)),('S',np.sin(x)**np.sin(x))]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(6.6,4.6))
for ax,(lab,y) in zip(axes.ravel(),sk):
    ax.plot(x,y,color='#2b6cb0'); ax.set_title(lab,fontsize=12,loc='left'); ax.set_ylim(0,1.05); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax.set_xticks([0,np.pi/6,np.pi/3,np.pi/2]); ax.set_xticklabels(['0','π/6','π/3','π/2'],fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

| | $(\cos x)^{\cos x}$ | $(\sin x)^{\sin x}$ | $(\cos x)^{\sin x}$ | $(\sin x)^{\cos x}$ |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **A** | P | Q | R | S |
| **B** | P | Q | S | R |
| **C** | Q | P | R | S |
| **D** | Q | P | S | R |
| **E** | R | S | P | Q |
| **F** | R | S | Q | P |
| **G** | S | R | P | Q |
| **H** | S | R | Q | P |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: E** — $(\cos x)^{\cos x}=R$, $(\sin x)^{\sin x}=S$, $(\cos x)^{\sin x}=P$, $(\sin x)^{\cos x}=Q$.

**Step 1 — endpoints.** As $x\to0$: $\cos x\to1,\ \sin x\to0$. As $x\to\tfrac\pi2$: the reverse.

**Step 2 — the two simple (monotone) ones.**

- $(\cos x)^{\sin x}$: $1^{0}=1\to 0^{1}=0$, so it **decreases** $1\to0$ = **P**.
- $(\sin x)^{\cos x}$: $0^{1}=0\to 1^{0}=1$, so it **increases** $0\to1$ = **Q**.

**Step 3 — the two $t^{t}$ ones (a dip to $\approx0.69$).**

- $(\cos x)^{\cos x}$: $t^{t}$ with $t=\cos x$ falling $1\to0$; the dip at $t=1/e$ is reached near the
  **right** = **R**.
- $(\sin x)^{\sin x}$: $t^{t}$ with $t=\sin x$ rising $0\to1$; the dip is near the **left** = **S**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(0.001,np.pi/2-0.001,400)
fns=[('(cos x)^cos x = R',np.cos(x)**np.cos(x)),('(sin x)^sin x = S',np.sin(x)**np.sin(x)),
     ('(cos x)^sin x = P',np.cos(x)**np.sin(x)),('(sin x)^cos x = Q',np.sin(x)**np.cos(x))]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(6.6,4.6))
for ax,(t,y) in zip(axes.ravel(),fns):
    ax.plot(x,y,color='#2b6cb0'); ax.set_title(t,fontsize=9); ax.set_ylim(0,1.05); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
    ax.set_xticks([0,np.pi/6,np.pi/3,np.pi/2]); ax.set_xticklabels(['0','π/6','π/3','π/2'],fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(the $t^{t}$ shape)*

::: {.question}
Sketch $y=x^{x}$ for $0<x\le1$: state its value as $x\to0^{+}$, its value at $x=1$, and where (and what) its
minimum is.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: starts at $1$, ends at $1$, minimum $\approx0.69$ at $x=1/e\approx0.37$ — a shallow U.**

**Step 1 — ends.** $x\to0^{+}$: $x^{x}=e^{x\ln x}\to e^{0}=1$ (since $x\ln x\to0$). At $x=1$: $1^{1}=1$.

**Step 2 — turning point.** $\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}x^{x}=x^{x}(\ln x+1)=0\Rightarrow\ln x=-1\Rightarrow
x=\dfrac1e$. There $y=\left(\tfrac1e\right)^{1/e}\approx0.69$ — a minimum (the only stationary point).

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(1e-4,1,400); y=x**x
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,3.0)); plt.plot(x,y,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
plt.plot(1/np.e,(1/np.e)**(1/np.e),'o',color='crimson')
plt.annotate('min ≈0.69 at x=1/e',(1/np.e,(1/np.e)**(1/np.e)),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(10,-4),fontsize=9,color='crimson')
plt.ylim(0.6,1.05); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y'); plt.title('y = xˣ on (0,1]',fontsize=10); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(count solutions from the shape)*

::: {.question}
How many solutions does $\;x^{x}=0.8\;$ have for $0<x\le1$? And $\;x^{x}=0.5$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: $x^{x}=0.8$ has $2$; $\;x^{x}=0.5$ has $0$.**

**Step 1 — recall the shape.** On $(0,1]$, $x^{x}$ falls from $1$ to its minimum $\approx0.69$ at $x=1/e$,
then rises back to $1$ — a U.

**Step 2 — read the level line across.**

- $y=0.8$ lies **between** the minimum $0.69$ and the top $1$, so it cuts the U **twice** (once on each side of
  $x=1/e$).
- $y=0.5$ lies **below** the minimum $0.69$, so it never meets the curve — **no** solutions.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import brentq
x=np.linspace(1e-4,1,400); y=x**x
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,3.1)); plt.plot(x,y,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y = x^x')
plt.axhline(0.8,color='#2ca02c',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='y=0.8 → 2 solutions')
plt.axhline(0.5,color='crimson',ls='--',lw=1.2,label='y=0.5 → 0 solutions')
xm=1/np.e
xL=brentq(lambda t:t**t-0.8,1e-4,xm); xR=brentq(lambda t:t**t-0.8,xm,1)
for xi in (xL,xR): plt.plot(xi,0.8,'o',color='#2ca02c',ms=5)
plt.plot(xm,xm**xm,'o',color='0.4',ms=4)
plt.ylim(0.45,1.03); plt.grid(alpha=0.25); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
plt.legend(fontsize=8,loc='upper center')
plt.title('a level line above the min cuts twice; below the min, never',fontsize=8.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q20 — maxima of a nested chain)*

::: {.question}
Let $\mathrm f_1=\cos x$, $\mathrm f_2=\sin(\cos x)$, $\mathrm f_3=\cos(\sin(\cos x))$,
$\mathrm f_4=\sin(\cos(\sin(\cos x)))$, $\mathrm f_5=\cos(\sin(\cos(\sin(\cos x))))$ (radians), with maxima
$m_1,\dots,m_5$. Which is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** all $=1$ &nbsp; **B** $0<m_5<m_4<m_3<m_2<m_1=1$ &nbsp; **C** $m_1=m_3=m_5=1,\ 0<m_2=m_4<1$
&nbsp; **D** $m_1=m_3=m_5=1,\ 0<m_4<m_2<1$ &nbsp; **E** $m_1=m_3=1,\ 0<m_2=m_4<1,\ 0<m_5<1$ &nbsp;
**F** $m_1=m_3=1,\ 0<m_4<m_2<1,\ 0<m_5<1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: E.** Track the **range** through each layer, and use that $\cos$ hits its max $1$ only when its
input is $0$, while $\sin$ on $[-1,1]$ is largest at $1$.

**Step 1 — $m_1$.** $\cos x$ reaches $1$ (at $x=0$). $m_1=1$.

**Step 2 — $m_2$.** $\cos x\in[-1,1]$; $\sin$ is increasing there, so $\max\sin(\cos x)=\sin(1)\approx0.84<1$.
$m_2=\sin 1$.

**Step 3 — $m_3$.** $\sin(\cos x)\in[-\sin1,\sin1]$, which **contains $0$**; $\cos$ of $0$ is $1$, and
$\sin(\cos x)=0$ is achievable ($\cos x=0$). So $m_3=1$.

**Step 4 — $m_4$.** $\cos(\sin(\cos x))\in[\cos1,1]$; $\sin$ of that peaks at $\sin1$. So $m_4=\sin 1=m_2$.

**Step 5 — $m_5$.** Now the inner $\sin(\cos(\sin(\cos x)))\in[\sin(\cos1),\sin1]\approx[0.62,0.84]$ — it
**never reaches $0$**, so the outer $\cos$ **cannot** reach $1$; $m_5=\cos(0.62)\approx0.81<1$.

So $m_1=m_3=1$, $\ 0<m_2=m_4<1$, $\ 0<m_5<1$ — **E**.
:::

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(MAT 2019 Q1C — a disguised standard curve)*

::: {.question}
*(MAT 2019 Q1C.)* For the values of $x$ at which it converges, the graph of
$\;y=\sin^{2}x+\sin^{4}x+\sin^{6}x+\sin^{8}x+\cdots\;$ is which of the following five graphs?
:::

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
def seg(ax,f,asy):
    bnds=[-180]+asy+[180]
    for lo,hi in zip(bnds[:-1],bnds[1:]):
        xd=np.linspace(lo+0.6,hi-0.6,500); ax.plot(xd,f(np.radians(xd)),color='#2b6cb0',lw=1.8)
    for a in asy:
        if -180<a<180: ax.axvline(a,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=0.8)
    ax.set_ylim(0,4); ax.set_xlim(-180,180)
    ax.set_xticks([-180,-90,0,90,180]); ax.set_xticklabels([-180,-90,0,90,180],fontsize=6)
    ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.6); ax.set_yticks([0,1]); ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
opts=[('(a)',lambda x:np.tan(x)**2,[-90,90]),
      ('(b)',lambda x:np.sin(x)**2,[]),
      ('(c)',lambda x:1/np.cos(x)**2,[-90,90]),
      ('(d)',lambda x:1/np.sin(x)**2,[0]),
      ('(e)',lambda x:1/np.tan(x)**2,[0])]
fig,axes=plt.subplots(3,2,figsize=(6.4,5.6)); ax=axes.ravel()
for i,(lab,f,asy) in enumerate(opts):
    seg(ax[i],f,asy); ax[i].set_title(lab,fontsize=11,loc='left')
ax[5].axis('off')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: (a) — the graph of $y=\tan^{2}x$.**

**Step 1 — recognise the geometric series.** It is geometric with first term $\sin^{2}x$ and ratio
$\sin^{2}x$ (with $\sin^{2}x<1$):
$$y=\frac{\sin^{2}x}{1-\sin^{2}x}=\frac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}=\tan^{2}x.$$

**Step 2 — read off the shape.** $\tan^{2}x\ge0$, is $0$ at $x=0$ and $x=\pm180^\circ$, equals $1$ at
$\pm45^\circ,\pm135^\circ$, and has **vertical asymptotes at $\pm90^\circ$** (where $\sin^{2}x\to1$). So the
correct sketch touches the axis at $0$ and $\pm180^\circ$ and shoots to $+\infty$ at $\pm90^\circ$ — that is
**(a)**.

**How the distractors differ** (all are neighbouring trig squares):

- **(b)** $\sin^{2}x$ — bounded between $0$ and $1$, no asymptotes.
- **(c)** $\sec^{2}x=1/\cos^{2}x$ — same $\pm90^\circ$ asymptotes as (a), but it never touches the axis (its
  minimum is $1$, at $0$ and $\pm180^\circ$).
- **(d)** $\csc^{2}x=1/\sin^{2}x$ — asymptotes at $0$ and $\pm180^\circ$; minimum $1$ at $\pm90^\circ$.
- **(e)** $\cot^{2}x=1/\tan^{2}x$ — zero at $\pm90^\circ$, with asymptotes at $0$ and $\pm180^\circ$.

Only (a) both **touches the axis at $0$** and **blows up at $\pm90^\circ$**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.figure(figsize=(5.4,3.0))
for lo,hi in [(-180,-90),(-90,90),(90,180)]:
    xd=np.linspace(lo+0.5,hi-0.5,400); x=np.radians(xd)
    plt.plot(xd,np.tan(x)**2,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
for a in (-90,90): plt.axvline(a,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1)
plt.ylim(0,4); plt.xlim(-180,180); plt.xticks([-180,-90,0,90,180])
plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8); plt.xlabel('x (degrees)'); plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('(a)  y = tan²x : 0 at 0, ±180; asymptotes at ±90',fontsize=10); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 6 &nbsp; *(PAT 2023 Q6 — transforming a parabola)*

::: {.question}
*Adapted from PAT 2023, Question 6.*

Let $f(x)=x^2$. A new graph $y=g(x)$ is obtained by taking the parabola, stretching it vertically by scale
factor $2$, making its line of symmetry $x=1$, and ensuring that it is never positive. Which formula is $g(x)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-2f(x-1)$ &nbsp; **B** $-f(x-1)$ &nbsp; **C** $-2f(x+1)$ &nbsp; **D** $-f(x+1)$
&nbsp; **E** $-f(2x-2)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: A.**

**Step 1 — line of symmetry.** The graph of $f(x-1)=(x-1)^2$ has vertex at $(1,0)$, so its line of symmetry is
$x=1$. That narrows the options to **A** or **B**.

**Step 2 — never positive.** A negative sign reflects the parabola in the $x$-axis, making it $\le0$ for all
$x$. Both **A** and **B** have that.

**Step 3 — vertical scale factor.** Stretching by scale factor $2$ means multiply the output by $2$. With the
reflection included, that gives
$$g(x)=-2(x-1)^2=-2f(x-1).$$
So the answer is **A**.
:::

## 4 · Converse & contrapositive

*Seeds: 2022 P2 Q5, Q17.*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — the three relatives of "if $P$ then $Q$"

1. **Write the three forms.**
   - **Converse:** swap — "if $Q$ then $P$".
   - **Contrapositive:** swap **and** negate — "if not $Q$ then not $P$".
   - **Inverse:** negate only — "if not $P$ then not $Q$".
2. **A statement and its contrapositive are equivalent** — same truth value, always. They stand or fall
   together.
3. **The converse is independent** — it may be true or false regardless. Test it by hunting a case with $Q$
   **true** but $P$ **false**.
4. **In a proof, watch the arrow's direction.** To conclude "$P\Rightarrow Q$" you need exactly that arrow —
   proving "$Q\Rightarrow$ (something)" leaves the job unfinished; you still owe its converse.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Worked idea.** Original: "multiple of $6\Rightarrow$ multiple of $3$" (true). Its **contrapositive** "not a
multiple of $3\Rightarrow$ not a multiple of $6$" is also true. Its **converse** "multiple of $3\Rightarrow$
multiple of $6$" is **false** ($3$). Equivalent partner, independent converse.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- Original: $P\Rightarrow Q$.
- Converse: $Q\Rightarrow P$.
- Contrapositive: $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$.
- Inverse: $\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q$.
- The original and contrapositive are always equivalent. The converse and inverse are always equivalent.
- A proof of the converse does **not** prove the original; always check the arrow direction.
- **Extra practice:** TMUA Logic and Proof notes for the language; MAT Section B and STEP Foundation for
  longer reasoning chains.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter, or "true / false" for each form with the reason or counterexample.
:::

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q5 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
A line $L$ passes through $(1,2)$. Let $P$ be the statement: *if the $y$-intercept of $L$ is negative, then
the $x$-intercept of $L$ is positive.* Which of these **must** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $P$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** the converse of $P$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** the contrapositive of $P$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I &nbsp; **C** II &nbsp; **D** III &nbsp; **E** I, II &nbsp; **F** I, III
&nbsp; **G** II, III &nbsp; **H** I, II, III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: F (I and III).**

**Step 1 — is $P$ true?** A line through $(1,2)$ with $y$-intercept $c<0$ has slope $\dfrac{2-c}{1-0}=2-c>0$.
Rising from $(0,c)$ with $c<0$, it crosses the axis at $x=\dfrac{-c}{2-c}>0$. So $P$ is **true**.

**Step 2 — the contrapositive.** It is logically equivalent to $P$, so it is **true** too. That gives I and
III.

**Step 3 — the converse.** "$x$-intercept positive $\Rightarrow$ $y$-intercept negative." Counterexample:
$y=-x+3$ passes through $(1,2)$, has $x$-intercept $3>0$ **and** $y$-intercept $3>0$. So the converse is
**false**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-1,4,200)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.6,3.2))
plt.plot(x,3*x-1,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y-int −1 (P): x-int +⅓')
plt.plot(x,-x+3,color='#dd6b20',lw=2,label='y=−x+3: x-int 3, y-int 3 (kills converse)')
plt.plot(1,2,'ko'); plt.annotate('(1,2)',(1,2),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,4))
plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.7); plt.axvline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.7)
plt.ylim(-3,5); plt.legend(fontsize=7.5); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y'); plt.title('lines through (1,2)',fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q17 — a direction error in a proof)*

::: {.question}
A student proves *"$x^{3}+ax^{2}+b=0$ has three distinct real roots **if** $27b\!\left(b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)<0$"* by:
**(I)** finding the stationary points $(0,b)$ and $\left(-\tfrac{2a}{3},\,b+\tfrac{4a^{3}}{27}\right)$;
**(II)** showing the condition puts one stationary point above the $x$-axis and one below;
**(III)** stating *"if the cubic has three distinct real roots then one stationary point is above and one
below"*;
**(IV)** concluding the condition gives three distinct roots.
Which best describes the proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** completely correct &nbsp; **B** it proves the converse of the whole statement &nbsp;
**C** wrong — II should follow III &nbsp; **D** wrong — needs the converse of the result in step II &nbsp;
**E** wrong — needs the converse of the result in step III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: E.**

**Step 1 — what does the conclusion need?** To reach IV ("condition $\Rightarrow$ three roots"), the missing
link is **"one point above and one below $\Rightarrow$ three distinct roots"**.

**Step 2 — what does the student actually state?** Step III is the **reverse**: "three roots $\Rightarrow$ one
above, one below". That's the converse of what's needed.

**Step 3 — the verdict.** Every line is *true*, but the argument uses the arrow the wrong way: it needs the
**converse of the result in step III** to close. So **E**. (Same converse trap as Q5 — a statement and its
converse are not interchangeable.)
:::

:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(write the three forms)*

::: {.question}
For "if $n$ is a multiple of $4$, then $n$ is even", write the **converse** and the **contrapositive**, and
say which of the three statements are true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: original true, contrapositive true, converse false.**

**Step 1 — original.** "Multiple of $4\Rightarrow$ even": true ($4k=2(2k)$).

**Step 2 — contrapositive** (swap and negate): "if $n$ is **odd**, then $n$ is **not** a multiple of $4$" —
**true** (equivalent to the true original).

**Step 3 — converse** (swap): "if $n$ is even, then $n$ is a multiple of $4$" — **false**: $6$ is even but
$6=4\times1+2$ is not a multiple of $4$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(which forms are equivalent?)*

::: {.question}
Which pairs among {original, converse, inverse, contrapositive} of "if $P$ then $Q$" **always** share the
same truth value?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: original $\equiv$ contrapositive, and converse $\equiv$ inverse.**

**Step 1 — original vs contrapositive.** "if $P$ then $Q$" $\equiv$ "if not $Q$ then not $P$" — always the
same truth value.

**Step 2 — converse vs inverse.** "if $Q$ then $P$" (converse) $\equiv$ "if not $P$ then not $Q$" (inverse),
because the inverse is the *contrapositive of the converse*.

**Step 3 — the two groups are independent.** Original and converse need **not** agree — that independence is
the whole point of these questions.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(the opposite pattern — true converse, false original)*

::: {.question}
Consider "if $x^{2}>x$ then $x>1$" (for real $x$). Is the statement true? Is its **converse** true?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: the statement is false; its converse is true.**

**Step 1 — solve the hypothesis.** $x^{2}>x\iff x^{2}-x>0\iff x(x-1)>0\iff x<0\ \textbf{or}\ x>1$.

**Step 2 — test the statement.** "$x^{2}>x\Rightarrow x>1$": take $x=-2$ — then $x^{2}=4>-2$ holds, but
$x>1$ is false. So the statement is **false** (it ignored the $x<0$ branch).

**Step 3 — test the converse.** "$x>1\Rightarrow x^{2}>x$": if $x>1$ then multiplying $x>1$ by $x>0$ gives
$x^{2}>x$. **True.** So here the *converse* holds while the original fails — the mirror image of Q5.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-2.2,2.2,400)
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,3.0))
plt.plot(x,x**2,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y=x²')
plt.plot(x,x,color='#dd6b20',lw=2,label='y=x')
for xv in (-2,1.6): plt.plot(xv,xv**2,'o',color='crimson')
plt.axvspan(-2.2,0,color='crimson',alpha=0.08); plt.axvspan(1,2.2,color='crimson',alpha=0.08)
plt.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.7); plt.axvline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.7)
plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('x²>x on the shaded x<0 or x>1',fontsize=10); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## 5 · Quantifiers & their order

*Seeds: 2022 P2 Q9, Q10, Q13.*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — read the quantifiers left to right

1. **Order is everything.** In "$\forall x\ \exists n\ \dots$" the $n$ may **depend on $x$** (you choose it
   after seeing $x$). In "$\exists x\ \forall n\ \dots$" one single $x$ must work for **every** $n$. Swapping
   $\forall$ and $\exists$ changes the meaning.
2. **To break a "$\forall$"**, find **one** bad case. **To prove a "$\exists$"**, exhibit **one** witness.
3. **"$\forall x$, if $P(x)$ then $Q(x)$" is false the moment one $x$ has $P$ true and $Q$ false** — test the
   extremes (very large / very negative $x$).
4. **"$\exists y$ with [expression in $y$] $<0$"**: read the expression as a **function of $y$**. If it is
   **non-constant linear** in $y$ it takes negative values, so the $\exists$ holds; the only escape is when
   the $y$-coefficient is $0$ (a constant).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Worked idea.** "$\forall x\ \exists n:\ x<n$" is **true** ($n$ depends on $x$ — pick $n=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$).
"$\exists x\ \forall n:\ x<n$" is **true** ($x=0$). But "$\forall x\ \forall n:\ x<n$" is **false** ($x=100,n=1$).
Same three ingredients, three different answers — all from the quantifier order.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- $\forall x\,\exists y$ means you may choose a new $y$ after seeing $x$.
- $\exists y\,\forall x$ means one fixed $y$ must work for every $x$.
- To prove an existence statement, give a **witness**.
- To break a universal statement, give a **counterexample**.
- If an expression is linear in the existential variable, e.g. $x+y(1-x)$, then a non-zero coefficient usually
  lets you make it as negative or positive as needed.
- **Extra practice:** TMUA Logic and Proof notes; MAT Section B reasoning; FP1/FP2 proof sections for
  quantifier order and witness/counterexample work.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter, with the witness or the counterexample.
:::

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q10 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
Which of these are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** for all real $x$ and all positive integers $n$, $\;x<n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** for all real $x$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $\;x<n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** there exists a real $x$ such that for all positive integers $n$, $\;x<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I &nbsp; **C** II &nbsp; **D** III &nbsp; **E** I, II &nbsp; **F** I, III
&nbsp; **G** II, III &nbsp; **H** I, II, III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: G (II and III).**

**Step 1 — I ($\forall x\,\forall n$).** One statement for **every** $x$ and $n$ at once. Counterexample
$x=100,\ n=1$: $100<1$ is false. So **I is false**.

**Step 2 — II ($\forall x\,\exists n$).** For each $x$ you may pick an $n$ **depending on $x$**: take
$n=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$ (or $n=1$ if $x<1$). A positive integer beyond any given $x$ always exists. **True.**

**Step 3 — III ($\exists x\,\forall n$).** Need **one** $x$ below every positive integer: $x=0$ works
($0<n$ for all $n\ge1$). **True.**
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q9 — break the "for all")*

::: {.question}
$(*)$: *for all real $x$, if $x<k$ then $x^{2}<k$.* Find the complete set of $k$ for which $(*)$ is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** no real numbers &nbsp; **B** $k>0$ &nbsp; **C** $k<1$ &nbsp; **D** $k\le1$ &nbsp;
**E** $0<k<1$ &nbsp; **F** $0<k\le1$ &nbsp; **G** all real numbers
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: A (no real numbers).**

**Step 1 — how could $(*)$ fail?** It is a "$\forall x$" of an implication; it breaks if **one** $x$ has
$x<k$ (hypothesis true) but $x^{2}\ge k$ (conclusion false).

**Step 2 — the extreme $x$.** For **any** $k$, take $x$ very negative (say $x=k-1000$): then $x<k$ is true,
but $x^{2}$ is enormous, so $x^{2}<k$ fails.

**Step 3 — conclusion.** That single $x$ breaks the "for all" for **every** $k$. So no value of $k$ makes
$(*)$ true.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-4,4,400); k=1.0
plt.figure(figsize=(4.8,3.0))
plt.plot(x,x**2,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2,label='y=x²')
plt.axhline(k,color='#dd6b20',ls='--',label='y=k')
plt.axvline(k,color='0.6',ls=':'); plt.plot(-3,9,'o',color='crimson')
plt.annotate('x<k but x²≫k',(-3,9),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,-4),color='crimson',fontsize=9)
plt.ylim(0,12); plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('a very negative x always breaks it',fontsize=10); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q13 — an $\exists y$ read as a function of $y$)*

::: {.question}
$(*)$: *there exists a real $y$ such that $x-xy+y$ is negative.* For how many real $x$ is $(*)$ true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** exactly one &nbsp; **C** exactly two &nbsp; **D** all except two &nbsp;
**E** all except one &nbsp; **F** all values
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: E (all except one).**

**Step 1 — group by $y$.** $x-xy+y=x+y(1-x)$ — a **linear function of $y$** with slope $(1-x)$.

**Step 2 — when can it be negative?** If $x\neq1$ the slope $(1-x)\neq0$, so as $y$ runs over the reals the
value runs over **all** reals — in particular it is negative for suitable $y$. So $(*)$ holds.

**Step 3 — the exception.** If $x=1$ the expression collapses to $1+y\cdot0=1$, a constant that is **never**
negative. So $(*)$ fails only at $x=1$ — true for **all $x$ except one**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(swapping the order flips the truth)*

::: {.question}
Classify each as true or false: **(a)** for all real $x$, there exists a real $y$ with $y>x$; **(b)** there
exists a real $y$ such that for all real $x$, $y>x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: (a) true, (b) false.**

**Step 1 — (a) $\forall x\,\exists y$.** For each $x$ choose $y=x+1$; then $y>x$. The $y$ **depends on $x$**,
which is allowed. **True.**

**Step 2 — (b) $\exists y\,\forall x$.** Now one fixed $y$ must beat **every** real $x$. But $x=y$ (or
$y+1$) already fails $y>x$ — there is no largest real. **False.**

**Step 3 — the moral.** The only change is the order of $\forall$ and $\exists$, and it flips the answer.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(an $\exists\forall$ that *is* true)*

::: {.question}
Is this true? *There exists a real $x$ such that for all real $y$, $\;xy=y$.*
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: true.**

**Step 1 — it's $\exists x\,\forall y$**, so one $x$ must work for **every** $y$.

**Step 2 — find the witness.** $x=1$: then $xy=1\cdot y=y$ for all $y$. One $x$ handles every $y$, so the
statement holds.

**Step 3 — contrast with Problem 4(b).** An $\exists\forall$ is true exactly when a **universal element**
exists ($x=1$ here); it is false when no single choice can cover all cases (no largest real there).
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}

## 6 · Counterexample & spot-the-error

*Seeds: 2022 P2 Q3, Q7, plus a real cross-exam problem (MAT 2022 Q1G).*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — one example to break it; the first line to break it

1. **To disprove "for all $n$, …", give ONE $n$** with the hypothesis **true** and the conclusion **false**.
   The example must obey the hypothesis — a case that fails the hypothesis proves nothing (a common decoy).
2. **To find the *first* error in a proof**, read top-down and stop at the earliest line that does not follow
   for **every** allowed value. A valid deduction *from* a false line is not the error.
3. **The headline trap: "the polynomial can't be factorised" $\neq$ "the number is prime".** An irreducible
   polynomial can still take composite values.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Worked idea.** $x^{2}+1$ is irreducible, yet $x=3$ gives $3^{2}+1=10=2\times5$ — composite. Polynomial
irreducibility says nothing about the primality of the numbers it produces.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- A counterexample to "$P\Rightarrow Q$" must have $P$ true and $Q$ false.
- If the hypothesis is false, it is **not** a counterexample.
- "Polynomial is irreducible" does not mean "every value is prime".
- For prime claims, try values that make the expression obviously divisible by a repeated constant, such as
  $n=40$ in $n^{2}+n+41$.
- In spot-the-error questions, find the **first invalid implication**, not just a later false conclusion.
- **Extra practice:** MAT Section B for proof-flaw questions; AMC 12 first 15 for quick counterexamples and
  divisibility traps.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter, with the counterexample or the guilty line.
:::

---

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q3 — find the counterexample)*

::: {.question}
Statement: *if $n$ is prime, then $n^{2}+2$ is not prime.* Which of these is a **counterexample**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $n=2$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** $n=3$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** $n=4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I &nbsp; **C** II &nbsp; **D** III &nbsp; **E** I, II &nbsp; **F** I, III
&nbsp; **G** II, III &nbsp; **H** I, II, III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: C (II only).**

**Step 1 — what a counterexample needs.** $n$ **prime** (hypothesis true) **and** $n^{2}+2$ **prime**
(conclusion false).

**Step 2 — test each.**

- $n=2$: prime, but $2^{2}+2=6$ is not prime — conclusion holds, so **not** a counterexample.
- $n=3$: prime, and $3^{2}+2=11$ **is** prime — hypothesis true, conclusion false — a **counterexample**. ✔
- $n=4$: $4$ is **not** prime, so it fails the hypothesis and cannot be a counterexample.

Only **II**.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q7 — the first error)*

::: {.question}
Claim: *the difference between two consecutive positive cube numbers is always prime.* Proof:
**(I)** $(x+1)^{3}=x^{3}+3x^{2}+3x+1$; **(II)** the difference is $3x^{2}+3x+1$; **(III)** $3x^{2}+3x+1$ has
no integer linear factors (negative discriminant); **(IV)** therefore $3x^{2}+3x+1$ cannot be factorised for
any positive integer $x$; **(V)** hence the difference is always prime. Best description?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** correct, claim true &nbsp; **B** correct, but counterexamples exist &nbsp; **C** first error
line I &nbsp; **D** line II &nbsp; **E** line III &nbsp; **F** line IV &nbsp; **G** line V
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: F (first error, line IV).**

**Step 1 — lines I–III are fine.** The *polynomial* $3x^{2}+3x+1$ has discriminant $9-12<0$, so it is
**irreducible** (no integer linear factors).

**Step 2 — the jump at IV.** "The polynomial doesn't factorise, so the **number** $3x^{2}+3x+1$ can never be
factorised (is prime)." That is the irreducible-$\neq$-prime trap.

**Step 3 — the counterexample.** $x=5$: $3(25)+15+1=91=7\times13$ — composite. So line IV is false (and V
follows from it), making **IV** the first error.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(break a famous "always prime")*

::: {.question}
Give a counterexample to *"$n^{2}+n+41$ is prime for every non-negative integer $n$"*.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: $n=40$ (also $n=41$).**

**Step 1 — where might a "$+41$" formula fail?** When $41$ divides the value — near $n=40$ or $n=41$.

**Step 2 — check.** $n=40$: $40^{2}+40+41=1681=41^{2}$ — composite. (Also $n=41$: $41^{2}+41+41=1763=41\times43$.)
So the claim fails, e.g. at $n=40$. (This is Euler's famous prime-rich polynomial — prime for $n=0,\dots,39$,
then it breaks.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(a Mersenne counterexample)*

::: {.question}
Give a counterexample to *"if $n$ is prime, then $2^{n}-1$ is prime"*.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: $n=11$.**

**Step 1 — hypothesis.** $n$ must be prime; $11$ is.

**Step 2 — conclusion fails.** $2^{11}-1=2047=23\times89$ — composite. So $n=11$ is prime while $2^{n}-1$ is
not: a counterexample. (Smaller primes $2,3,5,7$ all *do* give Mersenne primes, so you must go up to $11$.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(MAT 2022 Q1G — a genuine factorisation forces compositeness)*

::: {.question}
*(MAT 2022 Q1G.)* Given that $n^{4}+1=\left(n^{2}+\sqrt2\,n+1\right)\left(n^{2}-\sqrt2\,n+1\right)$, deduce
for how many positive whole numbers $n$ the value $n^{4}+4$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** never &nbsp; **(b)** exactly one &nbsp; **(c)** exactly two &nbsp; **(d)** exactly three
&nbsp; **(e)** infinitely many
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: (b) exactly one.**

**Step 1 — factorise $n^{4}+4$ the same way (Sophie Germain).**
$$n^{4}+4=(n^{2}+2)^{2}-(2n)^{2}=(n^{2}-2n+2)(n^{2}+2n+2).$$

**Step 2 — a product is prime only if a factor is $1$.** The smaller factor is $n^{2}-2n+2=(n-1)^{2}+1\ge1$,
and it equals $1$ **only at $n=1$**.

**Step 3 — evaluate.** At $n=1$, $n^{4}+4=5$ (prime). For every $n\ge2$ both factors exceed $1$, so the value
is composite. Prime for **exactly one** $n$ — **(b)**. (A genuine factorisation forces compositeness *except*
where a factor collapses to $1$ — the flip side of Q7.)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## 7 · Pigeonhole — "smallest $n$ that necessarily forces it"

*Seed: 2022 P2 Q8.*

::: {.callout-tip}
## The method — build the boxes, then add one

1. **"Smallest $n$ that *necessarily* forces $X$" is a pigeonhole question.** Group the pool into **boxes** so
   that two items from one box give $X$ (e.g. a pair that sums to the target).
2. **Find the largest selection that *avoids* $X$** — at most **one** item from each box, **plus** every
   "loner" that can never form $X$ (no partner, or a self-pair that isn't two *distinct* items). Call this
   maximum $m$.
3. **The answer is $m+1$** — one extra item must double up in a box.
4. **Count loners carefully** — they raise $m$, and forgetting them is the classic slip.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Worked idea.** Force two of $\{1,\dots,10\}$ to sum to $11$: the boxes are $(1,10),(2,9),(3,8),(4,7),(5,6)$
— $5$ pairs, no loners. Largest safe selection $=5$ (one per pair), so $6$ items force a pair.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Remember for next time

- Pigeonhole answers usually follow: **make boxes → find largest safe selection → add 1**.
- For sums, boxes are pairs with the required sum.
- For equal remainders, boxes are remainder classes.
- For fixed differences, boxes are pairs or chains separated by that difference.
- Count loners carefully: they can be included safely and increase the largest safe selection.
- **Extra practice:** AMC 12 first 15 for fast counting; MAT Section A for multiple-choice pigeonhole variants.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** A whole number $n$.
:::

---

### Problem 1 &nbsp; *(TMUA 2022 P2 Q8 — the seed)*

::: {.question}
$S$ is a selection of $n$ terms from $1,4,7,\dots,70$. Let $(*)$ be: *there are two distinct terms of $S$
summing to $74$.* What is the smallest $n$ for which $(*)$ is **necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** 12 &nbsp; **B** 13 &nbsp; **C** 14 &nbsp; **D** 21 &nbsp; **E** 22 &nbsp; **F** 23
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: C (14).**

**Step 1 — the pool.** The sequence is $3k-2$ for $k=1,\dots,24$ — **24 terms**.

**Step 2 — the boxes (pairs summing to $74$).** $(4,70),(7,67),\dots,(34,40)$ — **11 pairs**.

**Step 3 — the loners.** $1$ (its partner $73$ is not in the sequence) and $37$ (since $37+37$ is not two
*distinct* terms). Two loners.

**Step 4 — largest safe selection, then $+1$.** Take one from each pair plus both loners: $11+2=13$ terms with
no pair summing to $74$. So $13$ can still avoid $(*)$, but any **14** terms force a complete pair. Smallest
$n=\mathbf{14}$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 2 &nbsp; *(the same idea, small numbers)*

::: {.question}
From $\{1,2,\dots,10\}$, what is the smallest number of elements you must choose to be sure that **two of them
sum to $11$**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: 6.**

**Step 1 — make the right boxes.** Two numbers sum to $11$ exactly when they come from one of these pairs:
$$(1,10),(2,9),(3,8),(4,7),(5,6).$$
There are **5 pairs**, and every number belongs to exactly one pair, so there are **no loners** to add on.

**Step 2 — the largest safe choice.** If you choose one number from each pair, you can choose $5$ elements
without making a sum of $11$. For example, $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ is still safe.

**Step 3 — add one more.** A $6$th element has to land in a pair that is already represented, so it completes
a pair summing to $11$. Smallest $=\boxed{6}$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 3 &nbsp; *(plain pigeonhole)*

::: {.question}
How many people must be in a room to be certain that **at least two share a birth month**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: 13.**

**Step 1 — boxes.** The boxes are the $12$ birth months.

**Step 2 — safe maximum.** With $12$ people, it is still possible that everyone has a different birth month
(one person in each box).

**Step 3 — $+1$.** The $13$th person has nowhere new to go, so some month must contain at least two people.
Smallest $=\boxed{13}$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 4 &nbsp; *(pigeonhole by remainder)*

::: {.question}
From $\{1,2,\dots,50\}$, what is the smallest selection that **must** contain two numbers leaving the **same
remainder on division by $7$**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: 8.**

**Step 1 — boxes.** The possible remainders on division by $7$ are
$$0,1,2,3,4,5,6,$$
so there are **7 boxes**. Every selected number must go into exactly one of these boxes.

**Step 2 — safe maximum.** You could pick $7$ numbers with all different remainders, one from each box.

**Step 3 — $+1$.** An $8$th number must repeat one of the remainders. Therefore two chosen numbers have the
same remainder, and their difference is a multiple of $7$. Smallest $=\boxed{8}$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

### Problem 5 &nbsp; *(pigeonhole by difference)*

::: {.question}
From $\{1,2,\dots,10\}$, what is the smallest selection that **must** contain two numbers that **differ by
$5$**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Answer: 6.**

**Step 1 — boxes.** Numbers that differ by $5$ naturally pair up:
$$\{1,6\},\{2,7\},\{3,8\},\{4,9\},\{5,10\}.$$
There are **5 boxes**, and there are no loners.

**Step 2 — safe maximum.** You can choose one number from each box, giving $5$ numbers with no two differing
by $5$.

**Step 3 — $+1$.** A $6$th number must come from an already-used box, so it pairs with the number already
chosen from that box. Smallest $=\boxed{6}$.
:::
